# Vignette: Emmanuel

Emmanuel is a 72-year-old African man who has spent the better part of his adult life in service to the sea. He and his wife of forty-three years, Adaeze, live in a modest coastal home where the sound of water, once a source of deep pride, has become something he can no longer tolerate after dark.

Thirty-one years ago, Emmanuel was part of a Coast Guard response team dispatched to contain a chemical spill from a cargo vessel that had run aground in the harbor. He remembers the morning with a clarity that has never faded — the acrid, sweetish smell that hit him before the ship even came into view, the way his eyes began to water before he had time to register why. The team had been briefed that the hazard was minimal, that standard protective gear would be sufficient. It was not. Within hours, several crew members were vomiting on the deck. Emmanuel lost feeling in his hands. By the time the proper hazmat units arrived, he had been exposed for nearly four hours. He spent two weeks in hospital. The doctors told him he was lucky. He has never entirely believed them.

For years afterward, Emmanuel pushed forward. He returned to duty, raised three children, and carried the exposure the way he carried most difficult things — quietly, and alone. He retired from the Coast Guard at sixty-five with commendations and a ceremonial photograph that hangs in the hallway he now avoids walking through at night. The physical aftereffects — a persistent tremor in his left hand, recurring respiratory infections — became part of his ordinary life. He told himself the rest of it was ordinary too.

But in recent years, something has shifted. What he once managed through discipline and routine has begun to surface with a force he cannot contain. He wakes at three or four in the morning with his heart hammering, certain he can smell something chemical and wrong, though the room holds nothing but the salt air coming through the window. He lies rigid beside Adaeze, not waking her, running through what he knows to be true — that he is home, that it is over — but unable to feel the truth of it in his body. By morning he is exhausted and short-tempered in ways that shame him.

He no longer watches news coverage of industrial accidents or environmental disasters. Last spring, when a refinery fire was broadcast on the television his son had left on in the living room, Emmanuel walked out of the house and sat in his car in the driveway for two hours. He told no one why. He has developed a habit of checking the seals on windows before bed, though he cannot fully articulate what he believes he is keeping out.

Emmanuel is not a man who speaks easily about fear. He grew up in a culture and a profession that equated endurance with dignity, and he carries both with a kind of worn, careful pride. What troubles him most, he says, is not the nightmares or the sleeplessness but the feeling that his mind has become untrustworthy — that it replays the exposure not as memory but as ongoing fact, that some part of him is still standing on that deck, still breathing in what he should not have breathed. He finds himself irritable with Adaeze over small things and then flooded with guilt. He has pulled back from his grandchildren, worried that his agitation will frighten them, though the distance costs him something he struggles to name.

He came to therapy, he says, because Adaeze asked him to, and because at seventy-two he is tired — not of living, but of carrying something this heavy without knowing what to do with it. He sits in the chair with his hands folded and his posture straight, the bearing of a man still very much at his post, even as something behind his eyes makes clear how long he has been standing watch.
